Legal Notices in India — What You Need to Know
 

Understanding the legal framework behind each notice type helps you send one that will be taken seriously.

 
  
 
Rent Demand Notice
 

A rent demand notice is typically the first formal step before filing a suit for arrears of rent or eviction.
            It is governed by the applicable State Rent Control Act (e.g., Delhi Rent Control Act, Maharashtra Rent Control Act)
            and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Serving this notice via RPAD creates a paper trail that courts require.

 
  
 
Money Recovery Demand Letter
 

A demand letter is a prerequisite for most civil recovery suits in India. Under Order 37 of the CPC,
            summary suits for money recovery require that the defendant be given a chance to pay before a decree is passed.
            The limitation period for money recovery suits is 3 years from the date the debt became due (Limitation Act, 1963).

 
  
 
NDA Confidentiality Clause
 

NDAs are enforceable as contracts under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 if they meet the requirements of a valid
            contract (offer, acceptance, consideration, lawful object). Courts have enforced NDA breach claims under Sections
            55 and 73 of the Contract Act. Governing law should specify an Indian city for domestic enforceability.

 
  
 
Eviction Notice
 

Eviction in India is primarily governed by State Rent Control Acts. The notice must specify a valid ground for
            eviction as defined in the applicable state act (e.g., non-payment of rent, subletting without consent, personal
            bonafide need). A notice that does not cite a valid statutory ground can be invalidated in court.

 
  
 
Employment Termination Notice
 

Termination of employment in India is regulated by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for workmen and by the
            employment contract for non-workmen. For workmen in establishments with 100+ employees, prior government
            permission (Section 25N IDA) is required. Notice pay in lieu of the notice period is taxable as salary under
            Section 17(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

 
  
 
Cheque Dishonour (S.138 NI Act)
 

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds
            a criminal offence. Three strict deadlines apply: (1) the cheque must be presented within 3 months of issue;
            (2) this notice must be sent within 30 days of the bank dishonour memo; (3) the drawer has 15 days to pay after
            receiving this notice. Miss any deadline and the criminal complaint is not maintainable.

 
 
  
 
How to Send Legal Notices in India
 
     
  •   Registered Post with AD (RPAD): The strongest delivery method. The post office returns a signed acknowledgment card that is admissible as proof of service in Indian courts. 
    •  
  •   Speed Post: Accepted in most courts as proof of delivery. Faster than RPAD but tracking is not always reliable for smaller post offices. 
    •  
  •   Email: Legally recognised under the IT Act, 2000 if the recipient has consented to email communication. Use email only as a supplement, not a substitute, for RPAD for S.138 NI Act notices. 
    •  
  •   When to use a lawyer: For S.138 cheque bounce complaints, property disputes above ₹5 lakh, or any notice that may precede litigation — have a registered advocate review and sign the notice on your behalf. Lawyer-signed notices carry significantly more weight. 
    •  
 
 
 
  
 
Frequently Asked Questions
 
 
 
 
Is this legal notice legally valid in India?
  

A generated notice is a reference template, not a court-filed document. Legal notices under Indian law
            (CPC Section 80, NI Act Section 138) are valid when properly drafted, signed, and sent — ideally via
            Registered Post with Acknowledgment Due (RPAD). This tool generates the text; you are responsible for
            reviewing, signing, and dispatching it. For formal proceedings, have a registered advocate review the
            notice before sending.

 
 
 
 
 
What is a legal notice under Section 80 CPC?
  

Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) requires that before filing a civil suit against
            the Government of India or a Government officer, the claimant must serve a two-month notice. This notice
            must include the cause of action, relief sought, and the claimant's contact details. Failure to serve
            a Section 80 notice can result in the suit being dismissed.

 
 
 
 
 
Can I send this notice via email?
  

Email delivery is legally recognised under the Information Technology Act, 2000 if the recipient has
            consented to email communication or if there is a pre-existing email-based relationship. However, for
            maximum legal standing — especially for cheque dishonour notices under Section 138 NI Act — send by
            Registered Post with Acknowledgment Due (RPAD). RPAD creates an irrefutable delivery record admissible
            in court.

 
 
 
 
 
What is an NDA clause?
  

An NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) clause is a contractual obligation requiring one or both parties to
            keep specified information confidential for a defined period. A mutual NDA clause binds both parties
            equally. Under Indian law, NDAs are enforceable as contracts under the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
            The clause should specify: what information is confidential, the obligations of each party, exclusions
            (publicly available information), the confidentiality period, and the governing jurisdiction.

 
 
 
 
 
Does this tool store my information?
  

No. This tool runs entirely in your browser using JavaScript. No form data, personal names, amounts,
            or generated notice text is transmitted to any server. No cookies, localStorage, or analytics are used
            to capture notice content. Closing the browser tab permanently clears everything you entered.
